correctness.rationale: For every odd prime, the exact Fourier coefficient sums and sums of squares are verified. A random permutation of roots has correlation -1/m across different spectral modes; mixing with independent Haar phases yields -1/(p-1), exactly forcing uniform mean probabilities. A prime cyclotomic polynomial comparison proves no rational dependence among the m continuous-time eigenfrequency differences, so every positive-time tail is dense in the full spectral phase torus. The Haar barycenter is relative-interior, its midpoint with the root-permutation barycenter is relative-interior, and the elementary convex-density lemma plus Carathéodory give at most m+1 exact physical atoms. Every normalization and boundary p=3 are included; 592 finite exact rational checks and independent Fourier numerical tests supplement, not replace, the proof.

originality.rationale: The new exact finite-support uniform time-law, its simultaneous all-vertices quantification and ≤(p+1)/2 support bound are not present in the three highly relevant inspected primary full texts. The 2017 ε-uniform prime-cycle statement is strictly weaker because proximity to a target does not imply finite convex membership. The 2007 no-average theorem fixes the Cesàro law; the 2023 general sampling paper has no all-prime-cycle finite-support theorem. The explicit phase-correlation and relative-interior argument is the missing step. Targeted published-record searches found no stronger matching coverage, subject to the stated general-convexity overlap risk.

value.rationale: The theorem resolves exact arbitrarily late randomized observation-time uniform transport on every odd prime quantum ring with at most (p+1)/2 atoms, one law for all starting vertices. It establishes a substantive operational capability despite a known impossibility for every single observation time for p≥5, and separates optimized finite sampling from nonuniform Cesàro means. The natural graph family, exact uniform invariant and dimension-controlled atom bound provide motivation beyond standalone small computations.
